title: How to Use SUMIF in Excel (with Examples)
dek: SUMIF adds up only the numbers that meet a condition. The syntax is =SUMIF(range, criteria, [sum_range]) — like totaling sales for one region. Here is exactly how each part works, plus SUMIFS and wildcards.

intent.primaryKeyword: how to use sumif in excel

seo.metaTitle: How to Use SUMIF in Excel (with Examples)
seo.metaDescription: A clear SUMIF guide for Excel: syntax, real examples, number and text criteria, wildcards, and how SUMIFS adds up values with more than one condition.

richText: SUMIF is the function you reach for when a plain SUM is not enough — when you want to add only the numbers that meet a condition. Total the sales for one region, add only the expenses over a certain amount, sum the hours for one project: SUMIF does all of it with a single, readable formula.

body.richText: Point the criteria at a cell instead of typing it: =SUMIF(A2:A100, D1, B2:B100) totals whatever region you type in D1. One formula becomes a mini dashboard you can change on the fly.

items.question: What is the difference between SUMIF and SUMIFS in Excel?
items.answerRichText: SUMIF adds values that meet one condition, with the sum range last. SUMIFS handles several conditions at once and puts the sum range first. Use SUMIF for a single test and SUMIFS when two or more must all be true.

items.question: How do I use SUMIF with a date range?
items.answerRichText: Use SUMIFS with two date conditions, like =SUMIFS(B2:B100, A2:A100, ">="&DATE(2026,1,1), A2:A100, "<="&DATE(2026,3,31)) to total values within a quarter. The & joins the operator to the date so Excel reads it correctly.

items.question: Why is my SUMIF returning 0?
items.answerRichText: Usually the criteria does not match — a trailing space, different text, or numbers stored as text. Check that the range and criteria line up, and that "North" in the data exactly matches the "North" in your formula.
